column3: It states the decisive ground: Allah knows while people do not.
Attractive speech and claimed inward sincerity can conceal hostile contention.
It frames commanded fighting with a limit: fight those fighting you, without transgression.
Desisting is called better, showing that combat is not valued without its condition.
It marks destructive harm to cultivation and offspring as corruption, not good.
It concerns plotting after mercy, without clarifying the command or reversal in 2:216.
It repeats that one may dislike something in which Allah places much good.
It shows sinful pride can make a person reject a call to mindfulness.
It portrays fighting written upon a people and their later turning away from it.
It again grounds a practical command in Allah's knowledge beyond human knowledge.
It depicts giving oneself in seeking Allah's approval.
It classifies persistent disbelief but adds no relevant link to 2:216.
It repeats the contrast between Allah's knowledge and human non-knowledge.
It calls believers to enter submission wholly rather than follow the adversary's steps.
It exposes the human tendency to seek good endlessly and despair when evil touches him.
It warns against loving the spread of indecency and again invokes Allah's knowledge.
It presents Allah as mighty and wise after clear signs and possible slipping.
It names submission to Allah as occurring willingly or unwillingly.
It shows Allah's ruling over vulnerable rights and knowledge of every good deed.
It concerns the coming of Allah and the final return of affairs.
It directly notes believers' dislike of being sent out on a rightful occasion.
It gives prescribed limits while stating Allah knew their self-betrayal.
It warns of punishment for exchanging Allah's favor after clear signs.
It uses dislike rhetorically to condemn backbiting, without the good-evil reversal.
It concerns forgiveness after Joseph's brothers' wrongdoing.
It shows worldly life can be made attractive and thereby distort judgment.
It only names a written book.
It says people began knowing nothing, supporting humility about what they cannot see.
It presents revelation as Allah's means of judging disputes and guiding to truth.
It only mentions the growth of grain.
It directly joins fighting written upon people, their fearful reluctance, and the better hereafter.
It places severe hardship before entry into the Garden and affirms near divine help.
It contrasts the later state as better than the first.
It shows Allah knowing human limits while naming fighting among varied burdens and a greater good with Him.
It treats spending as good and affirms Allah's knowledge of every good deed.
It calls the disbelievers the worst of created beings, without the relevant comparison.
It calls Allah the best of judges in a family crisis.
It affirms Allah knows what people hide and disclose.
It records Allah sparing believers the fighting and turning opponents back without good.
It challenges any claim that people possess the unseen.
It distinguishes human love from Allah's knowledge of who is guided.
It reports people asking why they do not see those they counted evil.
It explicitly reverses an apparent good into evil for those who withhold it.
It names a victory and near opening that believers love.
It depicts Allah's exhaustive knowledge of the unseen and every hidden detail.
It prohibits preferring kinship allegiance when they prefer disbelief to faith.
It prohibits coercion and directs material support where good is recognized.
It only mentions the clarifying Book.
It states that hatred cannot prevent Allah from completing His light.
It depicts jealous preference and a mistaken judgment within a family.
It states Allah knows best what opponents say about the revelation.
It calls believers who do righteous deeds the best of created beings.
It connects patient believers with strength in fighting against those who do not understand.
It only swears by the clear Book.
It states that Allah establishes truth and nullifies falsehood despite criminals' dislike.
It criticizes love of the immediate and neglect of a weighty coming day.
It states that Allah establishes truth by His words despite criminals' dislike.
It gives a fighting command while grounding believers in Allah's companionship with the mindful.
It requires fulfillment of treaties with those who have not broken them, limiting conflict by conduct.
It only declares the Night of Decree better than a thousand months.
It joins future intention to Allah's will and asks for nearer right guidance.
It directly commands fighting in Allah's path and affirms His hearing and knowledge.
It concerns Allah's possible pardon for those unable to emigrate.
It asks whether opponents possess an earlier book to which they cling.
It calls for sincere worship despite disbelievers' dislike.
It commands moderation in eating and drinking.
It states that hatred cannot prevent Allah from perfecting His light.
It concerns reward for belief and righteous deeds.
It commands giving harvest dues and avoiding excess.
It makes love of Allah answerable in following the messenger.
It shows mention of fighting exposing fearful inner resistance to the command.
It rebukes love of the immediate life.
It seeks refuge from the evil of what He created.
It only mentions a protected Book.
It seeks refuge from the retreating whisperer.
It only mentions upright scriptures.
It condemns those who neither hear nor reason.
It parallels 2:216's wording of an obligation written upon you, though in a different duty.
It voices hope that the Lord may replace a lost thing with something better.
It distinguishes those not fighting or expelling believers, toward whom kindness and justice remain required.
It presents prayer as restraining indecency and wrong while Allah knows what people do.
It parallels the form of a prescribed duty written upon believers and gives its formative aim.
It applies Allah's knowledge of inner thoughts to a command of restraint and caution.
It only calls the recording angels noble scribes.
It shows human knowledge can diminish after it was possessed, while Allah remains knowing and powerful.
It states that Allah has prescribed mercy for Himself and will gather all for judgment.
It affirms Allah knows what people acquire by day and will report their deeds.
It makes fighting conditional on ending fitnah and forbids aggression once opponents desist.
It rebukes knowingly mixing and concealing truth.
It identifies preferring worldly life over the hereafter as a ruinous preference.
It grounds ultimate direction and return in Allah, not in human counsel.
It concerns appointed terms for destroyed towns.
It gives household eating permissions and greetings.
It calls the evil of listed acts detestable to the Lord.
It sets detailed provisions for a prescribed pilgrimage duty under Allah's warning.
It concerns the decreed destruction or punishment of towns before the Last Day.
It gives inheritance shares and related conditions.
It concerns envy over Allah's favor to Abraham's family.
It says conjecture cannot avail against truth, reinforcing the limits of unsupported judgment.
It labels a person as withholding good, transgressing, and doubtful.
It directly states Allah knows what human beings do not know.
It situates fighting within expulsion and fitnah, while requiring restraint when opponents desist.
It makes opponents' desisting decisive, linking cessation to Allah's forgiveness and mercy.
It limits response to equivalent transgression and joins it to mindfulness of Allah.
It directly weighs fighting against other grave harms and declares fitnah greater than killing.
It joins faith, migration, and striving in Allah's path with hope for His mercy.
It recounts those fleeing death in great numbers, then commands fighting in Allah's path.
It shows Allah's choice of leadership against people's objection and grounds it in His greater knowledge.
It portrays a military trial in which patience and Allah's permission, not numbers, determine endurance.
It gives the battle prayer for patience, firm footing, and help against denial.
It attributes victory to Allah's permission and describes His repelling of people through others.
It places the messenger arranging believers in their battle positions under Allah's hearing and knowledge.
It shows desire for what was promised preceding weakness and dispute in battle.
It contrasts anxious human assumptions about Allah with His possession of all command.
It identifies those who withdrew on the day of fighting and says Allah knows their concealed disbelief.
It turns a threat meant to produce fear into increased faith and reliance on Allah.
It denies people access to the unseen except as Allah chooses to disclose it.
It commands fighting for those who exchange worldly life for the Hereafter.
It frames fighting as rescue for oppressed men, women, and children seeking deliverance.
It commands the messenger to fight and urge believers, while Allah may restrain the deniers' force.
It requires verification in conflict and forbids judging a greeting of peace by worldly gain.
It distinguishes those who strive with wealth and selves from those who remain behind without excuse.
It compares shared suffering in pursuit of an enemy with believers' hope from Allah that opponents lack.
It forbids cooperation in sin and transgression, setting a moral boundary relevant to conflict.
It forbids hatred of a people from turning believers away from justice.
It forbids turning one's back when meeting those who disbelieve in battle.
It limits the prohibition of retreat by recognizing tactical movement and rejoining a force.
It commands firmness, frequent remembrance of Allah, and success when meeting a force.
It commands obedience, rejects dispute that causes loss of strength, and enjoins patience.
It directs preparation of strength and mounts to deter a hostile enemy known and unknown to believers.
It recognizes weakness while setting a divinely measured military burden and linking patience with Allah's presence.
It ties the aftermath of battle to an established divine order rather than mere worldly gain.
It challenges reluctance to fight those who broke oaths, began aggression, and sought expulsion.
It commands fighting and describes Allah's punishment, victory, healing, and removal of believers' anger through it.
It warns that love of kin, wealth, trade, and homes cannot outrank Allah, His messenger, and striving.
It rebukes heaviness when called to go forth and contrasts the worldly life with the Hereafter.
It warns that refusal to go forth brings replacement and punishment without harming Allah.
It recalls Allah's support in isolation, showing help is not dependent on visible numbers.
It commands going forth whether light or heavy and striving with wealth and selves as better.
It exposes those who rejoiced at staying behind and disliked striving in heat.
It records wealthy people seeking leave to remain behind when commanded to believe and strive.
It contrasts them with the messenger and believers who strive with wealth and selves and receive good.
It presents believers' selves and wealth as exchanged with Allah for the Garden through fighting in His path.
It counts thirst, fatigue, hunger, and every costly step in Allah's path as righteous deeds not lost.
It permits fighting for those wronged and affirms Allah's power to give them victory.
It identifies wrongful expulsion for saying Allah is Lord and depicts Allah's defense of those who support Him.
It commands striving for Allah with the striving due to Him while affirming no constriction in the religion.
It commands striving against deniers with the Quran in a great striving.
It states that whoever strives does so only for his own self, since Allah is independent of creation.
It promises guidance in Allah's ways to those who strive for Him.
It describes the crisis of forces gathering, eyes turning, and hearts reaching throats as a trial of believers.
It shows believers meeting the confederates with increased faith and submission to Allah's promise.
It gives the fighting sequence, its limits after subduing the enemy, and the divine testing within conflict.
It states that Allah will test believers until He makes known those who strive and remain patient.
It forbids weakness and calling for settlement from a position of superiority, grounding believers in Allah's presence.
It calls those who stayed behind to a coming fight against a mighty people, with obedience or punishment at stake.
It says that if deniers fought believers they would turn away and find no protector or helper.
It attributes the withholding of hands in the valley of Mecca to Allah after giving believers power over opponents.
It defines unhesitating faith through striving with wealth and selves in Allah's path.
It distinguishes spending and fighting before victory from doing so afterward, while promising good to both.
It forbids alliance with those who fought believers over religion, expelled them, or aided their expulsion.
It declares Allah's love for those who fight in His path in a firm, ordered formation.
It introduces a saving exchange whose elaboration is belief and striving with wealth and selves.
It names belief in Allah and His messenger and striving with wealth and selves as better for believers.
